analysis.one_liner: Bans former members of Congress from lobbying for life and extends staff lobbying bans to six years.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate committee that received it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for former senators, representatives, and elected congressional officers to ever lobby Congress after leaving office, up from the current two-year ban for senators and one-year ban for House members. It would extend the lobbying ban for most congressional staff from one to six years, bar registered lobbyists and foreign agents from working for the members or committees they lobbied for six years, create a searchable public website of lobbyist disclosures, require large lobbying firms to list the former members and senior staffers they hire, and raise the maximum civil penalty for violating lobbying disclosure rules from $200,000 to $500,000.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans, who currently face a system in which former lawmakers and senior staff sell their access to the same institutions they just left. Longer and lifetime bans, plus public disclosure of which lobbying firms employ ex-members and ex-staffers, would make that trade slower, more visible, and more costly.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a lifetime lobbying ban on former senators, House members, and elected congressional officers, replacing the current two-year (Senate) and one-year (House) cooling-off periods.
Extends the post-employment lobbying ban from one year to six years for most congressional staff, including personal, committee, and leadership staff.

Bars registered lobbyists and agents of foreign principals from being hired for six years by any member or committee they substantially lobbied, with waivers allowed only for compelling national need.

Requires large lobbying firms (those employing more than three registered lobbyists) to file annual public lists of former members and senior legislative officials they hire as employees, contractors, or paid consultants, posted to a searchable 'lobbyists.gov' database.
Raises the civil penalty for violating lobbying disclosure rules from $200,000 to $500,000 and directs filings to the U.S. Attorney for D.C. to catch underreporting.

analysis.who_pays: Lobbying firms and government-relations shops, which would lose their easiest recruiting pool of former lawmakers and senior staff and face new disclosure obligations and higher penalties; former members of Congress and senior staffers, who would lose a lucrative career path; and congressional offices, which would have a smaller pool of experienced lobbyists to hire.

drawbacks.text: Bans of this length can push influence-seeking into unregistered channels: former members who cannot lobby directly can still advise firms, strategize, and make introductions that are much harder to track, so the bill may shift the revolving door rather than close it.

The hiring ban and lifetime ban limit what former officials may do to earn a living after public service, an burden an honest supporter would acknowledge, and the six-year lobbyist-hiring ban can be waived by the ethics committees for 'compelling national need,' a potential loophole.
Longer cooling-off periods may discourage experienced people from serving on congressional staff at all, since the six-year restriction attaches to a wide range of ordinary staff jobs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and well-documented problem: former lawmakers and senior staff monetizing their access immediately after leaving office. The restrictions are strong and the disclosure provisions are genuinely useful to voters. The main design risk is that a lifetime ban may simply redirect influence work into consulting and advisory roles the bill does not reach, which is why the disclosure requirement for big lobbying firms is arguably its most effective piece. On balance the public benefit outweighs the cost, which falls on a small, well-paid industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never held a hearing or voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Tester introduced the bill on July 27, 2023, with Bennet as cosponsor, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never reported the bill, and no vote was held in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended.
Only two senators, both Democrats, signed on as cosponsors, so the bill had minimal support even within its own party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lobbying firms and former members of Congress are better off, since the existing short cooling-off periods and light disclosure rules stay in place. Nothing in the record shows an organized campaign against the bill; the decisive event was simply that the committee never acted.

against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred took no action on it; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no division can be measured; the only sponsor and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican or Democratic opposition was recorded.

industries.note: The bill would cut them off from their most valuable hires (former members and senior staff) for years or for life, force them to disclose those hires publicly, and raise penalties to $500,000. Their business depends on fast access to the lawmakers and staffers who just left, so its interest runs against the bill's public-transparency goal.

industries.industry: Consulting and advisory firms employing ex-lawmakers
industries.note: Firms that sign former members as paid consultants, a channel not always captured by current disclosure, would have to list those relationships annually on a public database and could face enforcement review for underreporting.

industries.industry: Former members of Congress and senior congressional staff
industries.note: A lifetime ban for members and a six-year ban for staff would close off the best-paying post-congressional career path for the people affected. For members this is a self-imposed limit on officeholders themselves, which is why it is central to the bill's anti-revolving-door purpose.
